```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# pct_eu() takes values already in per cent and rounds halves up, as the
# specification menu does, so that the pages agree
eu_curve <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
forks <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve_forks.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
devs <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_deviations.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_filter(curve == "positive")
eu_menu <- readr::read_csv("../data/menu_options.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
periods <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_periods.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
loo <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_loo.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
bailout <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_bailout.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
cnames <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_country_means.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("cntry", "country"))

# fixed decimals and a true minus sign
num <- \(x, d = 3) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f"), x) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct_eu <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(floor(x * 10^d + 0.5) / 10^d, format = "f", digits = d), "%")
minus <- \(x) gsub("-", "−", format(x), fixed = TRUE)

# shares of a set of curve rows below zero, and below zero with CR2 p < 0.05
below <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports)
below_sig <- \(d) 100 * mean(d$supports & d$sig)
fk <- \(ax, col = "share") forks[[col]][forks$axis == ax]
dv <- \(ax, op, col) devs[[col]][devs$axis == ax & devs$option == op & devs$rule == "cr2"]
eu_ref <- eu_curve |> datawizard::data_filter(is_reference)
twoway <- eu_curve |> datawizard::data_filter(estimator == "fe_twoway")
country <- eu_curve |> datawizard::data_filter(estimator == "fe_country")

# the displays of section 8.5: the reproduced specification and its country twin
is_ref_spec <- \(d) d$outcome == "mcosmo" & d$predictor == "unemp" & d$copredictor == "none" &
  d$pred_form == "raw"
per_ref <- \(smp, col) periods[[col]][is_ref_spec(periods) & periods$estimator == "fe_twoway" &
                                        periods$sample == smp]
per_unemp <- periods |> datawizard::data_filter(predictor == "unemp")
loo_two <- loo |> datawizard::data_filter(estimator == "fe_twoway", left_out != "none")
loo_cty <- loo |> datawizard::data_filter(estimator == "fe_country", left_out != "none")
vs <- \(cc) loo_two$variation_share[loo_two$left_out == cc]
ba <- \(grp, col) bailout[[col]][bailout$outcome == "mcosmo" & bailout$predictor == "unemp" &
                                   bailout$estimator == "fe_twoway" & bailout$group == grp]
design_label <- c(fe_twoway = "Two-way fixed effects", fe_country = "Country fixed effects")
```

The multiverse, or specification curve, is the method taught in the course, and this module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), which works on the Europeanisation and the economy case study, examines the origins of the idea, what is claimed for the method and the arguments now being made against it.

You run a multiverse yourself in the course, fixing a specification in a preregistration, fitting it and reading your result against the `r nrow(eu_curve)` specifications that make up the curve of the claim on the [Class results page](../class-results.qmd). The method is the subject of a live debate in 2025–26, in which serious objections have been raised against it, and the module aims to enable you to take a position in that debate.

## 1. Origins {#sec-origins}

The founding statement of the approach is a 2016 paper by Steegen, Tuerlinckx, Gelman and Vanpaemel [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse]. The authors start from the construction of the data before any model is fitted, observing that the conversion of raw data into an analysable dataset involves choices – which cases to exclude, how to code a variable, where to cut a scale – for which several options are usually reasonable. Rather than privileging a single dataset, Steegen and colleagues propose to build every dataset that a reasonable set of choices could have produced and to run the analysis on each, so that the reader learns how much the conclusion owes to decisions that nobody would defend as the only right ones. The idea is related to the 'garden of forking paths' described by @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience: a researcher who makes each choice once, on the fly, has walked a single path through a branching garden, and the p-value reached at the end retains no record of the branches. The 2016 paper states its ambition plainly, that "it should become standard practice to go beyond a single data set analysis and to acknowledge the multiverse of statistical results", and concedes at once what the critics would later press, that "performing a multiverse analysis will often be difficult, and to a large extent subjective" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710]. The authors also outlined the extension that a curve of models puts into practice, a *model* multiverse, in which "One specific analysis thus corresponds to a single sample from a model multiverse" [@SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, p. 710].

The multiverse presented in the original paper was *customised for critique*, in that the alternative datasets corresponded to choices that the original authors of the target study "might themselves have considered", drawn from their own prior publications. It was therefore a post-mortem on the flexibility of a single team rather than a general survey of the ways in which the question could be answered, a distinction that becomes relevant again in section 2. Steegen and colleagues also place the idea in an older lineage of perturbation and sensitivity analysis in economics and Bayesian statistics, to which the 2016 paper added the demand that the whole distribution of results be shown.

The modelling side was developed separately as **specification curve analysis** [@SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis], which enumerates the defensible ways of specifying a test, estimates all of them, plots the estimates in order and, in its full form, tests the curve as a whole against a null distribution built by permutation, that is, by reshuffling the data so that any true effect is removed. It is this display that the Specification curve page of the course adopts. A distinct strand kept the data and the question fixed and varied the *analysts*, from the 29 teams of the red-card study [@SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne] and the 73 teams in the study by @BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers to the 457 reanalysts of the SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness], among whose hundred claims is the claim of the Europeanisation case study, with its five reanalysts presented on the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-reanalysts). The two earlier studies are examined in detail in the [meta-analysis module](meta-analysis.qmd#sec-crowds). A further strand has proposed Bayesian hierarchical models for aggregating such data [@HoogeveenEtAl2020ImprovingStatisticalAnalysis]. The course combines these strands, treating the curve of the claim as a model multiverse and the five analysts of the robustness study, together with the class chart, as a many-analysts layer beside the curve, meant to be read against it.

## 2. Three purposes {#sec-purposes}

Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman pose the question around which the current debate is organised, namely what a multiverse is *for*. They distinguish three uses, "as a tool for reflection and critique, as a persuasive tool, as a serious inferential tool", and attach a failure to each: "it fails as a persuasive tool when researchers disagree about which variations should be included in the analysis", and "it fails as a serious inferential tool when the included analyses do not target a coherent estimand" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1]. Their conclusion is a mild one, in that the multiverse "does remain a valuable tool", but they "urge against taking it too seriously" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 1].

Each purpose imposes its own rules on how the set of specifications is built. A multiverse built for critique may mix analyses that answer slightly different questions, since its aim is to show that researchers plausibly disagree about the question, and "it may be perfectly sensible to include analyses with different estimands as long as it is plausible that researchers may try out different estimands" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. Such a set, however, cannot then be read as inference about a single quantity. Hullman states the condition in a companion blog post, writing that "what kinds of equivalence are needed will also depend on your goal in using a multiverse" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood].

It is for this reason that the course builds its artefacts to different rules. The [specification menu](../menu.qmd) of fourteen decisions, the [decision map](../menu.qmd#map) and the class chart serve reflection, making visible how far a result depends on decisions that look arbitrary from outside and presenting the options that answer other questions beside those that answer the claim. The curve of `r nrow(eu_curve)`, by contrast, is built to the standard that inference would require and is used to persuade, every specification on it being meant to answer the claim as the course reads it, while the two decisions that leave two estimands on the curve, the estimator and the predictor, are named as such. Section 8 examines the curve in the light of the arguments presented in sections 3 to 5.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Assign each artefact of the course to one of the three purposes: the specification menu, the preregistration of Task 5, the curve of `r nrow(eu_curve)`, the CR2 test that classes each specification, and the class chart. For each, write one sentence on what the set of specifications would have to look like for that purpose to be served. Note where one set of analyses is being used for two purposes.
:::

## 3. The pruning critique {#sec-auspurg}

The most direct empirical disagreement in the recent literature is that between a study of model uncertainty by Ganslmeier and Vlandas and Katrin Auspurg's reply to it. Crossing five dimensions of specification at once, across four literatures of political science, Ganslmeier and Vlandas produce about 3.6 billion estimates. They find that "the sign and statistical significance of estimates is more contingent on the underlying sample and the operationalization of indicators than on the inclusion of the control set" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6], and they formulate the dilemma themselves: "Running all possible models risks introducing errors in the empirical approach, but selecting a subset of robustness checks risks reintroducing the 'researcher's degree of freedom'" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 2].

Auspurg responds that "Multiverse analyses are only informative when all included models represent equally plausible strategies for estimating the same estimand" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. Her charge is that the models pooled by Ganslmeier and Vlandas are heterogeneous, in statistical quality and in what each estimates, their distribution thus combining numbers that cannot be compared. She distinguishes four kinds of nonequivalence: statistically inferior models ("Many models do not include fixed effects or cluster-robust SE, which are standard in panel data analyses" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]); unstable country subsets; causal misspecification from randomly combined covariates; and measurement nonequivalence, where "Outcomes differ in scope … and are sometimes negatively correlated. This clearly indicates that they do not reflect the same construct" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1]. When the set is restricted to the 1,152 models that she classes as justified, against 91,008 unjustified ones, a 60/40 split among the significant coefficients becomes one in which 97% point the same way. She rules out the selection of models by their fit, noting that "Ironically, the authors' own fit criterion (AIC) consistently favors unjustified models" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 1], and places the remedy before estimation, in "thorough, theory-based model selection" [@Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed, p. 2]. The constructive version of the same demand appears as the rule of estimand consistency in Young and Cumberworth's book, under which "any 'necessary control' requires a clear causal diagram or definitional justification supported by prior research" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 57]. The two authors are also explicit that "there is nothing in the distribution of estimates per se that tells us which is the true effect" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 119].

## 4. One correct analysis {#sec-lakens}

Lakens, Rasti and Tunç push the criticism further, taking as their target the inference that many people draw from analytic variability, namely that, since reasonable analyses disagree, there is no single correct analysis and researchers should report distributions instead. The three authors separate random variation, quantified by standard errors, from uncertainty about which auxiliary assumptions are true – which measure is valid, which units belong in the sample, which adjustment set is right – and argue that the second kind of uncertainty is reduced by research rather than absorbed by wider intervals. In their view, once the auxiliary assumptions are fixed, "there is a fact of the matter about which analysis correctly implements that test" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 7], robustness "is a consequence of valid tests, and not a goal in itself" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 15], and "Variability across specifications based on uninformed hunches, especially when less plausible alternatives are included, provides little actionable insight" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 10].

Task 5, in which you fix one specification before running it, may seem to offer an answer to Lakens and colleagues, but the two devices solve different problems. Preregistration addresses a problem of timing, ruling out the choice of a specification after seeing where the numbers fall, which is a real worry, given that "in the absence of preregistration, researchers may as well determine what is equivalent based on whether or not it supports their result" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 5]. The argument advanced by Lakens and colleagues concerns warrant, which does not depend on timing, since an arbitrary choice remains arbitrary when it is preregistered. Two caveats weigh against the device used by the course itself. Preregistering a reanalysis of data that already exist is a weaker form of preregistration, since "[w]hen the data already exist, authors can explore the data prior to registering their analysis" [@YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, p. 149]. The two approaches can also be combined: "one could preregister a multiverse analysis to combine the strengths of both approaches" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9].

## 5. Frequency and probability {#sec-reading}

One practical rule drawn from the literature that criticises the method concerns how a curve is to be *read*, and it prohibits the treatment of frequency as probability. The share of specifications supporting the claim describes a curated set of analyses and is not the probability that the claim is true. Rohrer and colleagues ask for variation to be "treated possibilistically", any result found anywhere in a justified set being a live possibility, and they attach a condition to this reading: "This possibilistic interpretation is only sensible if every universe included is indeed deemed justified" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 6]. The Milliways project shows how standard displays emphasise how *often* an outcome occurs, thereby inviting "misleading, probabilistic conclusions" [@SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses]. Lakens and colleagues put the point most bluntly: "Scientists should not compute the percentage of agreement across different data-analytic strategies, because we do not resolve scientific disagreement by majority vote" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 16].

The live class chart on the Class results page, where every submitted specification appears as a mark over the curve, is arguably best read as a many-analysts demonstration, the classroom analogue of the 29 and the 73 teams, with the further property that every declared specification was fixed in a preregistration before it was run. Heyman and Vanpaemel, who conduct multiverse projects with students, describe the design as "comparable to the many-analysts-one-dataset approach used by Silberzahn et al. (2018)", and note that when several analysts each make their own choices "there is a multiverse of multiverse analyses" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 7].

## 6. Robustness and replicability {#sec-replicability}

SCORE, the programme that produced the robustness study, subjected claims to three kinds of repetition [@AlipourfardEtAl2021SystematizingConfidenceOpen]. A reproduction repeats the original analysis on the original data, a robustness check applies different but defensible analyses to the same data, and a replication asks the same question of new data. In that sense a multiverse, however large, is a robustness check, every one of its specifications being fitted to the same sample, so that a chance feature of that sample would be found by every specification together. The specifications do not constitute independent tests, and their agreement is evidence about the analysis, given the data.

The specifications on the Europeanisation curve agree on the direction of the association but divide on the strength of the evidence (section 8.4). The replication of the claim in the SCORE replicability study, on later Eurobarometer waves, found a positive coefficient that was not significant, the opposite of the sign predicted by the claim, and SCORE judged the replication not successful, an outcome of which the curve could not have warned. The specifications on the curve vary the analysis while holding the sample fixed, so that their agreement says nothing about how far a new sample might differ, which is what the confidence interval of any single specification describes, and robustness to analytic choices and replicability are therefore separate properties of a finding.

## 7. The multiverse in the classroom {#sec-teaching}

The usefulness of the multiverse in teaching is accepted on every side of the debate. Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman concede that "the multiverse has been a valuable training tool" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 8], and Heyman and Vanpaemel build their teaching on it, formulating two rules that the course follows. The first rule places the reasons before the number of paths: "the goal should not be to merely devise as many paths as possible", and "[t]he key is that the alternatives are properly motivated" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 4]. It is because of this rule that every option of the menu carries a reason, while the second rule is pastoral: "one should be cautious that students do not completely lose faith in (psychological) science" [@HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom, p. 9]. A day that follows a published claim through every defensible analysis, only to learn that a replication on new data did not succeed, could leave a class cynical. The case study can also be read the other way, however, as research working as it should, in which five analysts and a class could check the claim and a replication could test it.

Hullman offers a further reason why this literacy will matter more, observing that building a multiverse is becoming cheap, because "lots of forms of robustness checking that used to be difficult are now trivially easy" [@Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood] once software can generate the specifications. When anyone can produce a curve on demand, the skill that is likely to remain scarce lies in judging what belongs in it, naming the purpose that it serves, and refusing the readings that its construction cannot support.

## 8. The Europeanisation curve {#sec-europeanisation}

The Europeanisation case study allows the debate to be followed on a curve of `r nrow(eu_curve)` specifications, built from a menu of fourteen decisions, along which the strength of the evidence varies with those decisions. The claim of the case study, taken from an article published in 2016 [@Teney2016DoesEUEconomic], is that "poor economic performances ... decrease positive dimensions of EU framing" (p. 619). The subsections below examine that curve in the light of the arguments of sections 3 to 5, the last of them presenting the displays that the course retains beside it. This section accompanies [the inference reading](../curve.qmd#inference) of the case study, which addresses a single narrow question, namely what a test of the curve as a whole can and cannot establish.

### 8.1 Pruning a menu of fourteen decisions {#sec-eu-pruning}

The Europeanisation case study applied Auspurg's test, and the stricter standard set by Rohrer and colleagues for a multiverse used for inference, to its own menu, every option of every decision being asked whether it is a justifiable way of answering the claim as the course reads it. The options that failed this test left the curve without leaving the course. Three of the categories distinguished by Auspurg reappeared on that menu. The pooled estimator, fitted without country effects, falls in her first category, as do the conventional standard errors of the fixed-effects designs, which treat the ten years of a country as independent. The curve therefore retains the two fixed-effects designs and classes every point by CR2 errors clustered by country with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, as the [module on panel data](panel-data.qmd#sec-inference) explains. The four restricted samples are versions of her second category, and the findings that these samples carry are retained in the displays of section 8.5. Her fourth category, measurement nonequivalence, applied to the outcome axis of the full menu, on which six framing scales of different scope stood in for 'EU framing'.

As the four scales used in the paper are shares of a single instrument, summing to one for each respondent who mentions anything, a confirmation of the claim on a negative scale largely counts the result on the positive scales a second time. For this reason the curve retains the three positive scales named by the claim, scored as shares, while the negative scales have a curve of their own, as [the measurement module](measurement.qmd#sec-negative) works through and the section on the frame set in the [specification menu](../menu.qmd#frame-set) records.

@fig-off-curve shows the effect of each option that left the curve when it is swapped into every specification on the curve, with everything else held as it was. The reason recorded for each option in the list on which the specification menu draws (`data/menu_options.csv`) is one of three: the option answers another question, it answers this question less well because an assumption that it needs fails on these data, or it is a check of an answer that the curve already contains.

```{r}
#| label: fig-off-curve
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: !expr 'paste0("Options that left the curve of the claim, each swapped into the specifications of the curve to which it applies: the share of the refitted specifications that lie below zero with p < 0.05. The vertical line marks the curve itself (", pct_eu(below_sig(eu_curve)), "). Each option is tested under the rule that fits it: CR2 errors with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom for linear models fitted by least squares and for the within–between model, and errors clustered by country on 26 degrees of freedom for random effects, the beta family and the imputed variants. The two imputation engines cover 24 specifications; the count stands for the rate, whose t and partial correlation are identical. Sources: `data/menu_deviations.csv`, `data/menu_options.csv`.")'
judgement_label <- c(other_question = "answers another question",
                     weaker_answer = "answers this question less well",
                     check = "a check of an answer on the eu_curve")
rule_kept <- c("cr2", "re_cr1_g1", "rewb_cr2", "beta_cr1_g1", "mi_rubin_cr1_g1")
off <- devs |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!on_curve, axis != "se", option != "rate", rule %in% rule_kept) |>
  dplyr::left_join(eu_menu |> datawizard::data_select(select = c("axis", "option", "label", "judgement")), by = c("axis", "option")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(judgement = factor(judgement_label[judgement], judgement_label),
         label = reorder(label, below_zero_sig))
ggplot2::ggplot(off, ggplot2::aes(below_zero_sig, label, colour = judgement)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = below_sig(eu_curve), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_segment(ggplot2::aes(x = 0, xend = below_zero_sig, yend = label), linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(size = 2.2) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c("#0e3b6a", "#0f6b6b", "#8c5a10"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100), labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  ggplot2::guides(colour = ggplot2::guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "below zero with p < 0.05", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Read against Auspurg's argument, the pruning changes the picture in the direction that her reply to Ganslmeier and Vlandas leads one to expect. Of the specifications on the curve, `r pct_eu(below(eu_curve))` lie below zero and `r pct_eu(below_sig(eu_curve))` lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05. The options that answer other questions reduce the share the most, pooled OLS to `r pct_eu(dv("estimator", "pooled_cl", "below_zero_sig"))` and the exclusion of the bailout countries to `r pct_eu(dv("sample", "no_bailout", "below_zero_sig"))`, while the options that answer the same question in another way remain close to the curve, among them the split rule for silent respondents at `r pct_eu(dv("noop", "split", "below_zero_sig"))`. The options that left the curve remain on the menu, the decision map and the class chart as material for reflection, each with its reason attached. That is a disclosure, and disclosure does not supply the justification demanded by Auspurg, which lies instead in the reasons that a reader can contest option by option.

::: {.callout-tip}

Pick one decision of the [specification menu](../menu.qmd) and write Auspurg's case for pruning it. Which of her four nonequivalence categories applies, and what would the curve look like if the decision were fixed at its best-justified option? Then write the case for keeping it, in Rohrer, Hullman and Gelman's terms: which purpose does varying this decision serve? The estimator and the sample are the two decisions where both cases are strong. Compare what you have written with the reason that the menu gives for each option.

### 8.2 One correct analysis on the curve of the claim {#sec-eu-lakens}

The pruning described in section 8.1 moves some way towards the position taken by Lakens and colleagues. The inference rule of the curve, for instance, was decided on evidence about the data – the year-to-year correlation of the residuals within a country and the few countries that account for most of the variation – rather than by convention, which is the kind of empirical work on an auxiliary assumption that these authors ask for. The pruning stops short of that position on the estimator, however, the curve retaining two designs because the claim, as written, does not say whether the changes common to all of Europe belong to the comparison, a question that the argument advanced by Lakens and colleagues would require the analyst to settle before the test.

### 8.3 The fork chart {#sec-eu-forks}

The fork chart drawn for the Europeanisation case study decomposes, decision by decision, the variance of the claim-aligned partial correlation across the `r nrow(eu_curve)` specifications on the curve. Of this variance the estimator accounts for `r pct_eu(fk("estimator"))`, the predictor for `r pct_eu(fk("predictor"))`, the choice among the three positive scales for `r pct_eu(fk("outcome"))` and the adjustment set for `r pct_eu(fk("copredictor"))`, while the decisions of measurement together account for a few per cent and the interactions between decisions for `r pct_eu(fk("interactions"))`. A change of the estimator alone alters whether a specification lies below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 in `r pct_eu(fk("estimator", "crossing_rate"))` of the pairs, and a change of the predictor alone in `r pct_eu(fk("predictor", "crossing_rate"))`.

Numbers like these, when put to the critics, invite a particular over-claim, namely that the dispersion on the curve is estimator dispersion rather than estimand dispersion, so that Auspurg's diagnosis no longer applies. The critics would reply that the estimator fork *is* an estimand fork in their sense, and on this curve the course concurs with them. The two remaining designs both compare a country with itself over time, but the two-way design does so relative to the common European path of each year, whereas the design with country effects alone retains the changes through which every member state went together. The two designs thus answer related but different questions, as the [module on panel data](panel-data.qmd#sec-two-designs) explains. The curve retains both designs because both are defensible readings of the claim, naming them as two estimands rather than presenting their spread as uncertainty about a single quantity. The predictor is a fork of the same kind, since unemployment and GDP growth are two measures of 'poor national economic performance' between which the claim does not choose.

The decomposition arguably supports a more modest reading, in which it *locates* where the argument has to take place, and every party to the debate endorses that use. Lakens and colleagues "support the use of multimodel analyses to hypothesize about 'which analytical decisions are most consequential'" [@LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne, p. 6], Ganslmeier and Vlandas present their method as something that "can help inform which combinations of choices are more or less warranted" [@GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources, p. 6], and Steegen and colleagues promised pointers to the most consequential choices from the start. Read in this way, the fork chart indicates which decisions on the menu require a theory. A large estimator share means that you have to decide whether your question concerns change relative to the common European path or all change within a country, and a large predictor share means that you have to decide which measure of the economy the claim is about.

### 8.4 The strength of the evidence {#sec-eu-reading}

The rule stated in section 5 applies directly to the curve of the case study. The share of the specifications on the Europeanisation curve that support the claim – `r pct_eu(below(eu_curve))` below zero on the curve of `r nrow(eu_curve)`, `r pct_eu(below_sig(eu_curve))` below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 – describes a curated set of analyses and is not the probability that the claim is true.

Whenever these shares are quoted in the course, they describe the curve that you are looking at, and the [inference reading](../curve.qmd#inference) exists to police the boundary between that description and any claim about evidence. For the permutation test designed in that reading, the consequence is that a probabilistic device, the permutation p-value, is applied to an object which, according to the current literature, should be read possibilistically. The inference reading explains what the test licenses under its sharp null, the hypothesis that the effect is zero in every unit, while this module adds a warning about everything that the test does not license.

Rohrer and colleagues also observe that a multiverse persuades only under a precondition: "This can only work if the results are fairly unambiguous across specifications" [@RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood, p. 3]. On the curve of the claim the direction of the association meets that precondition, but the strength of the evidence does not, since whether a specification clears the 5% threshold depends mainly on the estimator. Of the specifications with country effects alone, `r pct_eu(below_sig(country))` lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05, against `r pct_eu(below_sig(twoway))` of the two-way ones, and the reproduced specification itself has a CR2 p-value of `r num(eu_ref$p_cr2)`. The curve may therefore persuade a reader that the association runs in the direction of the claim within countries, while leaving open whether the evidence is strong once the changes common to all of Europe are removed, a question about the estimand as much as about the data. The threshold itself is referred by the CR2 test to the variation among the countries, as the [module on panel data](panel-data.qmd#sec-inference) explains. If you ever build a multiverse to defend a result of your own, this is the precondition to check before you rely on it.

In the sense of section 5, the class chart of the case study is a many-analysts demonstration, on which every declared specification, fixed in the Task 5 preregistration before it was run, is drawn in black, and the specifications tried with `try_spec()` and submitted with `submit_exploration()` in Task 4 are drawn in green. On this curve the class will not agree on the strength of the evidence and may not agree on the direction. Disagreement among the analysts in a class is no verdict on robustness in either direction, but it does demonstrate that the dispersion documented by the many-analysts literature is real, reproducible and, once the menu and the preregistrations are on the table, *explainable*. The chart therefore serves reflection, practised as a group, which also answers anyone who asks why the class chart is allowed to straddle zero.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open [the Class results page](../class-results.qmd) and find the black mark for the specification that you declared in Task 5 (or the reproduced specification, if you did not submit one). First read its neighbourhood possibilistically: what is the full range of aligned estimates among specifications that differ from yours on exactly one decision? Then catch yourself the moment you start counting – 'most of my neighbours agree with me' – and write one sentence on what that count would and would not establish, given how this universe was built.
:::

### 8.5 Heterogeneity and influence {#sec-heterogeneity}

The four sample restrictions on the Europeanisation menu left the curve because each changes the population about which the claim is made, but the findings obtained under these restrictions belong in the course and are retained in three displays. Each display answers a question that a curve of one population cannot answer, namely where and when in that population the association is found, and none of the three adds a point to the curve.

In @fig-periods the 36 core specifications of the curve – the three positive scales on raw or logged unemployment or on growth, with or without the other measure of the economy, under both fixed-effects designs – are fitted on the full panel and on each half of it.

```{r}
#| label: fig-periods
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-cap: "The 36 core specifications of the curve on the full panel and on each half of it, by design. Open circles have CR2 p < 0.05 and crosses p ≥ 0.05; the lines join the fits of one specification, and the burgundy line is the reproduced specification and its twin with country effects alone. The vertical axis is the claim-aligned partial correlation, so below zero is the direction of the claim. Source: `data/display_periods.csv`."
per_plot <- periods |>
  datawizard::data_modify(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label),
         period = factor(sample, c("all", "y2004_2008", "y2009_2013"),
                         c("2004–2013", "2004–2008", "2009–2013")),
         p_class = dplyr::if_else(p_cr2 < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05"),
         spec = paste(outcome, predictor, copredictor, pred_form),
         reproduced = is_ref_spec(periods))
ggplot2::ggplot(per_plot, ggplot2::aes(period, r_ca, group = spec)) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  ggplot2::geom_line(colour = "#0e3b6a", linewidth = 0.3, alpha = 0.25) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(shape = p_class), colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2, alpha = 0.5) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(data = datawizard::data_filter(per_plot, reproduced), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(data = datawizard::data_filter(per_plot, reproduced), ggplot2::aes(shape = p_class),
             colour = "#8b1538", size = 2.4) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = 1, "p ≥ 0.05" = 4), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = minus) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(design)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "claim-aligned partial r") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

For the reproduced specification the slope is `r num(per_ref("all", "b"), 5)` on the full panel (CR2 p = `r num(per_ref("all", "p_cr2"))`), `r num(per_ref("y2004_2008", "b"), 5)` on 2004–2008 (p = `r num(per_ref("y2004_2008", "p_cr2"), 4)`) and `r num(per_ref("y2009_2013", "b"), 5)` on 2009–2013 (p = `r num(per_ref("y2009_2013", "p_cr2"))`), each half on its own thus yielding a steeper slope than the panel as a whole. Among the 24 unemployment specifications, `r pct_eu(below_sig(dplyr::filter(per_unemp, sample == "all")))` lie below zero with CR2 p < 0.05 on the full panel, `r pct_eu(below_sig(dplyr::filter(per_unemp, sample == "y2004_2008")))` on 2004–2008 and `r pct_eu(below_sig(dplyr::filter(per_unemp, sample == "y2009_2013")))` on 2009–2013. Neither half provides a second answer to whether framing changed with the crisis. The earlier window contains no crisis, and its slope therefore describes how framing tracked the smaller fluctuations of those years, while the later one drops the comparison with the years before the crisis and asks how framing moved with the deepening and easing of the crisis once it had begun. Taken together, the two halves suggest that the association is not confined to the crisis years and that it was somewhat stronger once the crisis had started.

In @fig-loo one country at a time is left out of the reproduced specification and of its twin with country effects alone. The variation from which the two-way slope is identified is concentrated in a few countries: once the fixed effects are removed, Greece accounts for `r pct_eu(vs("GR"))` of the remaining variation in unemployment, Spain for `r pct_eu(vs("ES"))`, Poland for `r pct_eu(vs("PL"))` and Ireland for `r pct_eu(vs("IE"))`.

```{r}
#| label: fig-loo
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| fig-cap: "The slope of the cosmopolitan share on unemployment with one country left out at a time, under each design. Open circles have CR2 p < 0.05 and crosses p ≥ 0.05; the burgundy line marks the slope on all 27 countries. Countries are ordered by the two-way slope without them. Source: `data/display_loo.csv`."
country_order <- loo_two |>
  dplyr::left_join(cnames, by = c("left_out" = "cntry")) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange("-b") |>
  dplyr::pull(country)
loo_plot <- loo |>
  datawizard::data_filter(left_out != "none") |>
  dplyr::left_join(cnames, by = c("left_out" = "cntry")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label),
         country = factor(country, country_order),
         p_class = dplyr::if_else(p_cr2 < 0.05, "p < 0.05", "p ≥ 0.05"))
loo_full <- loo |>
  datawizard::data_filter(left_out == "none") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(design = factor(design_label[estimator], design_label))
ggplot2::ggplot(loo_plot, ggplot2::aes(b, country)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey70") +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(data = loo_full, ggplot2::aes(xintercept = b), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.6) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(shape = p_class), colour = "#0e3b6a", size = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_shape_manual(values = c("p < 0.05" = 1, "p ≥ 0.05" = 4), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = minus, n.breaks = 4) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(design), scales = "free_x") +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "slope per point of unemployment, without the country", y = "country left out") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

With one country left out, the two-way slope ranges between `r num(min(loo_two$b), 5)` (without `r cnames$country[cnames$cntry == loo_two$left_out[which.min(loo_two$b)]]`) and `r num(max(loo_two$b), 5)` (without `r cnames$country[cnames$cntry == loo_two$left_out[which.max(loo_two$b)]]`). Under the CR2 test, `r sum(loo_two$p_cr2 < 0.05)` of the 27 two-way refits reach p < 0.05, although the full panel does not (p = `r num(per_ref("all", "p_cr2"))`), and `r sum(loo_cty$p_cr2 < 0.05)` of the 27 refits with country effects alone do. The display puts the complete set of exclusions in place of a single hand-picked one, such as the exclusion of Greece and Spain together, and its 27 refits are 27 checks of one answer rather than 27 answers.

In @tbl-bailout the three positive scales are fitted on unemployment separately in the eight countries that received financial assistance and in the other nineteen, and the difference between the two groups is tested in one model on all 270 cells. With eight clusters, the Satterthwaite degrees of freedom of the CR2 test fall to between `r num(min(bailout$df_cr2[bailout$group == "bailout"]), 1)` and `r num(max(bailout$df_cr2[bailout$group == "bailout"]), 1)` for the bailout countries, making the test for this group strict.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-bailout
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "Slopes on unemployment in the eight bailout countries (Cyprus, Greece, Hungary, Ireland, Latvia, Portugal, Romania, Spain), in the other nineteen, and the difference between the two, estimated in one model on all 270 cells with an interaction. CR2 p-values in brackets, on Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Source: `data/display_bailout.csv`."
bailout |>
  datawizard::data_filter(predictor == "unemp") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(cell = paste0(num(b, 5), " (", num(p_cr2), ")")) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("outcome", "estimator", "group", "cell")) |>
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = cell) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(outcome = factor(outcome, c("mcosmo", "mutil", "mpos")),
         estimator = factor(estimator, names(design_label))) |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("outcome", "estimator")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(Scale = c(mcosmo = "cosmopolitan", mutil = "utilitarian",
                      mpos = "positive composite")[as.character(outcome)],
            Design = design_label[as.character(estimator)],
            `Bailout countries` = bailout, `Other countries` = other,
            Difference = difference) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:5, align = "r") |>
  tinytable::style_tt(fontsize = 0.8)
```

For the reproduced specification the slope is `r num(ba("bailout", "b"), 5)` in the bailout countries (CR2 p = `r num(ba("bailout", "p_cr2"))`, on `r num(ba("bailout", "df_cr2"), 1)` degrees of freedom) and +`r num(ba("other", "b"), 5)` in the others (p = `r num(ba("other", "p_cr2"), 2)`, on `r num(ba("other", "df_cr2"), 1)`), and the difference of `r num(ba("difference", "b"), 5)` has CR2 p = `r num(ba("difference", "p_cr2"))`. The same pattern is found for the cosmopolitan share and the positive composite under the two-way design, but not for the utilitarian scale.

Taken together, the three displays suggest that the association between unemployment and positive framing is concentrated in the countries in which the crisis was deepest and appears in both halves of the decade, which is what a reader of the claim needs to know about it. The displays are kept off the curve for the reason given in section 2, since a curve that mixed the full panel with its halves and its subsets would count answers about different populations as votes on a single question.

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The debate read here: @GanslmeierVlandas2025EstimatingExtentSources and the reply by @Auspurg2025RobustnessBetterAssessed; @RohrerEtAl2026WhatsMultiverseGood with the companion post by @Hullman2026WhatMultiverseGood; and @LakensEtAl2026ThereOnlyOne. The origins: @SteegenEtAl2016IncreasingTransparencyMultiverse, @GelmanLoken2014StatisticalCrisisScience and @SimonsohnEtAl2020SpecificationCurveAnalysis, with a framework for judging which analytic decisions are equivalent in @DelGiudiceGangestad2021TravelersGuideMultiverse. The many-analysts strand: @SilberzahnEtAl2018ManyAnalystsOne, @BreznauEtAl2022ObservingManyResearchers and @AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, and, for the diagnosis that many disagreements between analysts are disagreements about the estimand, @AuspurgBruderl2021HasCredibilitySocial. The book-length guide is @YoungCumberworth2025MultiverseAnalysisComputational, the tools are @SarmaEtAl2023MultiverseMultiplexingAlternative and @SarmaEtAl2024MilliwaysTamingMultiverses, and the classroom design is @HeymanVanpaemel2022MultiverseAnalysesClassroom. Quotations from the PsyArXiv preprints are cited by the pagination of the preprints. The numbers on this page are computed, when the page is built, from files written by the case-study pipeline: the curve `data/spec_curve.csv` and its decomposition `spec_curve_forks.csv`, the comparison of every option with its twins on the curve in `menu_deviations.csv`, the reasons in `menu_options.csv`, and the displays `display_periods.csv`, `display_loo.csv` and `display_bailout.csv`, described in the [codebook of the displays](../data/displays_codebook.md).
